items.title: Inflation, Interest Rates, and the Power of Central Banks
items.zh: 通货膨胀、利率与中央银行的力量
items.summary: 通胀从哪里来、央行怎么用利率"踩刹车"和"踩油门"、加息为什么会影响房贷、股市和就业，以及历史上的经验教训。读懂财经新闻的核心词汇。
paras: Few economic forces affect ordinary people as directly as inflation. When prices rise faster than incomes, families notice it immediately: at the supermarket, at the gas station, and when the rent increases. Yet the institutions that are most responsible for managing inflation, central banks, operate largely out of public view, and the tools they use can seem mysterious. This article explains what inflation is, why it happens, how central banks attempt to control it, and why their decisions matter to everyone, from homeowners and workers to investors.
What is inflation?

Inflation is a sustained increase in the general level of prices across an economy. The key word is "general." If the price of coffee rises because of a poor harvest in Brazil, that is a change in a relative price, not necessarily inflation. Inflation occurs when the prices of most goods and services rise together over time, meaning that each unit of currency buys less than it did before. In other words, inflation reduces the purchasing power of money.

Governments measure inflation using price indexes. In the United States, the most widely cited measure is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, which tracks the cost of a representative "basket" of goods and services purchased by typical households, including food, housing, transportation, clothing, medical care, and entertainment. Each month, statisticians collect tens of thousands of prices and calculate how much the cost of the basket has changed. Economists also pay close attention to "core inflation," which excludes food and energy prices, because those prices are particularly volatile and can obscure the underlying trend.

The opposite of inflation is deflation, a general decline in prices. Although falling prices might sound attractive, sustained deflation can be economically dangerous. If consumers expect prices to keep falling, they may postpone purchases, which reduces demand, which in turn causes businesses to cut production and employment. Japan experienced prolonged periods of mild deflation and weak growth from the 1990s onward, an experience that has made many policymakers wary of allowing inflation to fall too low.
Why does inflation happen?
Economists generally identify several causes of inflation, which often operate simultaneously.

Demand-pull inflation occurs when total demand in an economy exceeds what the economy can produce. When consumers, businesses, and governments all want to spend more, but the supply of goods and workers cannot keep up, sellers raise prices. This can happen during strong economic booms, or when governments inject large amounts of money into the economy.

Cost-push inflation occurs when the costs of production rise, forcing businesses to raise prices. A sharp increase in the price of oil, for example, raises transportation and manufacturing costs across the entire economy. Supply chain disruptions, such as those experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic, can have a similar effect.

Expectations also play a crucial role. If workers expect prices to rise by five percent next year, they will demand wage increases of at least five percent. If businesses expect their costs to rise, they will raise their prices in advance. In this way, expectations of inflation can become self-fulfilling, producing what economists call a "wage-price spiral." This is one reason why central banks care so much about their credibility.

Finally, over long periods, inflation is closely connected to the growth of the money supply. As the economist Milton Friedman famously argued, inflation is, in the long run, "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon." When the quantity of money grows much faster than the quantity of goods and services, the value of each unit of money tends to fall.
Is some inflation good?

Most central banks in advanced economies do not aim for zero inflation. Instead, many target an annual inflation rate of around two percent. Moderate inflation is generally considered healthy, provided that it remains stable and predictable. There are several reasons for this. A small positive rate of inflation provides a buffer against the dangers of deflation. It makes it easier for wages and prices to adjust, since it is psychologically easier for employers to give smaller raises than to cut wages. And it gives central banks more room to lower interest rates during a recession.

High and unpredictable inflation, by contrast, causes serious harm. It erodes the value of savings, especially for people who keep their money in cash or low-interest accounts. It hurts people on fixed incomes, such as many retirees. It makes long-term planning difficult for businesses. And in extreme cases, known as hyperinflation, it can destroy an economy. In Germany in 1923, prices doubled every few days; workers were paid twice a day and rushed to spend their wages before they lost their value. More recently, Zimbabwe and Venezuela have experienced hyperinflation, with devastating consequences for their populations.
What do central banks do?

A central bank is an institution responsible for managing a country's currency, money supply, and interest rates. Examples include the Federal Reserve in the United States, the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, and the People's Bank of China. Most central banks in democratic countries operate with a significant degree of independence from elected governments. The rationale is that politicians, facing elections, might be tempted to stimulate the economy in the short term at the cost of higher inflation later.

The Federal Reserve operates under what is known as a "dual mandate": to promote maximum employment and stable prices. Other central banks, such as the European Central Bank, have price stability as their primary objective.
The main tool: interest rates

The most important tool of most central banks is the short-term interest rate. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target for the federal funds rate, the rate at which banks lend to one another overnight. Changes in this rate ripple outward through the entire financial system, influencing the interest rates on mortgages, car loans, credit cards, business loans, and savings accounts.

The logic is straightforward. The higher the interest rate, the more expensive it becomes to borrow. A rise in interest rates tends to reduce borrowing. Households postpone buying homes and cars; businesses delay investment projects; consumers spend less on credit. At the same time, saving becomes more attractive, because savings accounts and bonds pay higher returns. The overall effect is to reduce demand in the economy, which eases the upward pressure on prices. This is often described as "tightening" monetary policy, or "putting on the brakes."

Conversely, when the economy is weak and inflation is low, central banks lower interest rates to encourage borrowing, spending, and investment. This is described as "loosening" or "easing" monetary policy, or "pressing the accelerator."

The difficulty is that monetary policy works with long and variable lags. A change in interest rates today may not have its full effect on the economy for a year or more. Central bankers must therefore make decisions based on forecasts of where the economy is heading, not merely on where it is now. Former Federal Reserve chair William McChesney Martin famously described the central bank's job as "to take away the punch bowl just as the party gets going," meaning that it must sometimes slow the economy before inflation has fully appeared.
Other tools

When interest rates are already close to zero, central banks cannot easily lower them further. During the global financial crisis of 2008 and again during the pandemic in 2020, many central banks turned to unconventional tools. The most significant was quantitative easing, in which the central bank creates new money to purchase large quantities of government bonds and other financial assets. This pushes down longer-term interest rates and increases liquidity in the financial system. Central banks also use "forward guidance," publicly communicating their likely future policy in order to shape expectations. Because expectations matter so much, a central bank's words can sometimes be almost as powerful as its actions.
How interest rates affect markets and households
Changes in interest rates affect asset prices throughout the economy.

Bonds. When interest rates rise, newly issued bonds pay higher yields, so existing bonds with lower yields become less attractive, and their prices fall. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Stocks. Higher interest rates tend to put pressure on stock prices for several reasons. They increase borrowing costs for companies, which can reduce profits. They make safer investments such as bonds relatively more attractive. And in valuation models, future profits are "discounted" back to the present using an interest rate; the higher the rate, the lower the present value of those future profits. This effect is particularly strong for fast-growing companies whose profits are expected far in the future, which helps explain why technology stocks are often especially sensitive to changes in interest rates.

Housing. Mortgage rates are closely linked to broader interest rates. When rates rise, monthly payments on new mortgages increase substantially, which reduces the number of people who can afford to buy a home and tends to cool the housing market.

Currencies. Higher interest rates can attract foreign investment, increasing demand for a country's currency and strengthening its exchange rate. A stronger currency makes imports cheaper, which can help reduce inflation, but it also makes exports more expensive for foreign buyers.
The risks of getting it wrong
Central banking is often described as more art than science, and mistakes can be costly.

If a central bank keeps interest rates too low for too long, it may allow inflation to become entrenched. In the 1970s, a combination of oil price shocks and overly loose monetary policy produced a decade of high inflation in the United States and many other countries. Inflation was finally brought under control only when Federal Reserve chair Paul Volcker raised interest rates to nearly twenty percent in the early 1980s. The policy worked, but at a severe cost: the United States experienced a deep recession, with unemployment rising above ten percent.

If, on the other hand, a central bank raises rates too aggressively, it may push the economy into an unnecessary recession, causing job losses and business failures. Some economists argue that the Great Depression of the 1930s was made far worse by tight monetary policy, and that the crisis could have been prevented, or at least greatly reduced, had central banks acted differently.

The ideal outcome, which central bankers call a "soft landing," is to reduce inflation without causing a recession. Historically, soft landings have proved difficult to achieve, although not impossible.
The inflation surge of the early 2020s

The early 2020s provided a dramatic real-world test. As economies reopened after pandemic lockdowns, demand surged, supported by large government spending programs and very low interest rates. At the same time, supply chains were severely disrupted, and energy prices spiked, particularly after the outbreak of war in Ukraine. Prices rose sharply, eroding the purchasing power of savings. In 2022, inflation in the United States reached its highest level in about forty years, and many other countries experienced similar increases.

Central banks initially described the inflation as "transitory," expecting it to fade as supply problems were resolved. When it persisted, they responded with some of the fastest interest rate increases in decades. Mortgage rates roughly doubled within a year. Stock and bond markets fell significantly in 2022. The episode prompted vigorous debate among economists about whether central banks had reacted too slowly, and about the relative importance of demand and supply factors. Inflation subsequently declined considerably, and the debate over the lessons of this period continues.
Why it matters to you

Even if you never read a central bank statement, monetary policy shapes your financial life. It influences whether you can afford a home, how much interest you earn on savings, how much you pay on loans, how your investments perform, and, ultimately, how secure your job is. Understanding the basic relationships between inflation, interest rates, and asset prices allows you to read financial news with greater understanding, to recognize why markets react so strongly to a single sentence from a central bank chair, and to make more informed decisions about borrowing, saving, and investing. In an economy where the value of money itself is constantly shifting, that understanding is a form of protection.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
items.zh: 人工智能与工作的未来
items.summary: 从历史上的技术革命说起，分析 AI 会替代、改变还是创造哪些工作，对不同行业和技能的影响，以及个人、企业和政府该如何应对。大学阶段科技与社会议题的高频学术词汇。
paras: Every major technological revolution has been accompanied by anxiety about the future of work. In the early nineteenth century, English textile workers known as the Luddites smashed mechanical looms that they feared would destroy their livelihoods. In the 1930s, the economist John Maynard Keynes warned of "technological unemployment." In the 1960s, the United States government established a commission to study whether automation would cause mass joblessness. Each time, the fears proved at least partly mistaken. Jobs were destroyed, sometimes in enormous numbers, but new ones were created, and overall employment continued to grow.

Today, the arrival of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence has revived these debates with new intensity. Systems that can write, translate, summarize documents, generate images, analyze data, write computer code, and hold conversations are now widely available. Unlike previous waves of automation, which mainly affected manual and routine tasks, AI appears capable of performing many tasks that were previously considered the exclusive domain of educated professionals. This raises a question that is both economically important and personally urgent for millions of people: is this time different?
Lessons from history
To understand what might happen, it is useful to examine how previous technologies have affected work. Economists generally distinguish between several effects.

The displacement effect occurs when technology performs tasks that were previously done by human workers, reducing the demand for those workers. Tractors and combine harvesters, for example, dramatically reduced the number of people needed in agriculture. In 1900, around forty percent of American workers were employed on farms. Today, the figure is below two percent.

The productivity effect occurs when technology makes workers more productive, reducing costs and prices, which increases demand for goods and services and therefore for the workers who produce them. Cheaper food meant that families could spend more money on other things, creating jobs in manufacturing, retail, and services.

The reinstatement effect occurs when technology creates entirely new tasks and occupations. Many of today's most common jobs, such as software developer, digital marketing specialist, and data analyst, did not exist a few decades ago. Research by economists has found that a large share of today's jobs are in occupations that did not exist in 1940.

Despite the fact that automation has destroyed many jobs, total employment has continued to grow. However, historical experience also offers a less comforting lesson. Even when the long-term outcome is positive, the transition can be painful. The workers who lose their jobs are often not the same people who obtain the new ones. Displaced workers may lack the skills required by emerging industries, or live in regions where new jobs are not being created. The decline of manufacturing in parts of the United States and Europe, driven by both automation and globalization, left lasting economic and social damage in many communities.
What makes AI different?
Several features of current AI systems suggest that their impact may differ from that of earlier technologies.
First, AI is a general-purpose technology. Like electricity or the internet, it can be applied across almost every industry, rather than affecting only a single sector.

Second, AI affects cognitive tasks. Previous automation mainly replaced physical labor and highly routine mental tasks, such as calculation and filing. Modern AI systems can perform tasks involving language, judgment, and pattern recognition that require considerable education. Some studies have found that occupations requiring a university degree may be more exposed to large language models than many manual occupations, which reverses the pattern of earlier automation.

Third, the pace of change may be unusually rapid. Steam power and electricity took decades to spread through the economy, because they required enormous investments in new factories and infrastructure. AI software, by contrast, can be distributed to millions of users almost instantly.

Nevertheless, there are reasons for caution about dramatic predictions. Exposure to AI does not necessarily mean replacement. A task being technically possible for a machine does not mean that it will be economically worthwhile, legally permitted, or socially accepted for the machine to perform it. Adoption also depends on organizational change, which tends to be slow. Many businesses still struggle to make effective use of technologies that have been available for decades.
Replacement or augmentation?
A crucial distinction in current debates is between automation, in which machines replace human workers, and augmentation, in which machines assist human workers and make them more productive.

Most jobs consist of many different tasks. A doctor, for example, examines patients, interprets test results, makes diagnoses, explains treatment options, provides reassurance, writes reports, and manages administrative paperwork. AI might perform some of these tasks well, such as analyzing medical images or drafting reports, while being much less suitable for others, such as comforting a frightened patient or making a difficult ethical judgment. In such cases, AI is more likely to change the nature of the job than to eliminate it. Many jobs are likely to be transformed rather than eliminated.

Early studies of AI in the workplace offer some evidence of augmentation. In one widely discussed study of customer service agents, access to an AI assistant increased productivity, with the largest improvements among less experienced workers. Similar results have been reported for some writing and programming tasks. With machines handling routine tasks, workers can focus on more complex problems, on interpersonal interaction, and on creative work.

However, augmentation and replacement are not always clearly separate. If AI makes each worker significantly more productive, a company may choose to employ fewer workers to produce the same output, rather than producing more. Which outcome occurs depends on factors such as demand for the product, competition, and the decisions of managers.
Which jobs are most affected?

Predictions about specific occupations vary widely, and many have proved inaccurate in the past. Whether these predictions will prove accurate remains uncertain. Nevertheless, some general patterns can be identified.

Tasks that are highly structured, involve processing large amounts of text or data, and follow predictable patterns appear most exposed. These include some forms of data entry, basic translation, routine writing, customer support, bookkeeping, and certain types of administrative and clerical work.

Tasks that require physical dexterity in unpredictable environments, such as plumbing, electrical work, caregiving, and many forms of construction, have so far proved difficult to automate, although advances in robotics may eventually change this. Interestingly, some physically demanding occupations may prove more resilient than some office jobs.

Tasks that depend heavily on human relationships, trust, empathy, and physical presence, such as nursing, teaching young children, counseling, and many forms of management and negotiation, also appear relatively resistant to full automation.

In logistics and transportation, AI and automation are already widespread: route optimization, demand forecasting, automated warehouses, and computer vision systems that read container numbers and license plates. Self-driving trucks have been tested extensively, although widespread deployment has proved slower and more difficult than many predicted a decade ago, owing to technical, regulatory, and safety challenges.
A view from the warehouse yard

Consider how these forces are already playing out in a single industry. In a large distribution center, AI-driven software now forecasts demand, decides where each product should be stored, and calculates the most efficient route for every forklift and picker. At the gates, cameras automatically read container numbers and license plates, a task that once required a worker with a clipboard. Yet the yard still depends heavily on people. Someone must verify the cases where the camera is uncertain, inspect damaged seals, photograph containers for insurance claims, coordinate with drivers who arrive late or at the wrong door, and solve the countless small problems that no system anticipated. In practice, the technology has removed some of the most repetitive parts of these jobs while increasing the importance of judgment, communication, and the ability to work with digital systems. Workers who learn to use the new tools, and who understand the whole process well enough to notice when the software is wrong, have become more valuable rather than less. Those whose roles consisted almost entirely of routine data entry have faced greater pressure. This pattern, in which technology reshapes tasks within an occupation rather than simply eliminating it, appears in many other sectors as well, from banking to healthcare.
The question of inequality

One of the most important questions about AI concerns not the total number of jobs but the distribution of benefits. If the productivity gains from AI flow mainly to the owners of technology companies and to highly skilled workers, existing inequalities could widen considerably. If, on the other hand, AI raises the productivity of less experienced workers more than that of experts, as some early studies suggest, it could potentially reduce certain inequalities.

The outcome is not determined by technology alone. It depends heavily on policy choices, on the bargaining power of workers, on competition between firms, and on how organizations decide to use the technology. As several economists have emphasized, technology is not destiny; societies can shape the direction of technological change.
Ethical and practical concerns

The spread of AI in the workplace also raises a range of ethical issues. AI systems used in hiring may reproduce or amplify biases present in historical data, disadvantaging certain groups of applicants. Algorithmic management, in which software assigns tasks, monitors performance, and even recommends disciplinary action, can leave workers feeling surveilled and powerless, particularly when decisions are not transparent. When an AI system makes a mistake, questions of accountability become complicated: who is responsible, the developer, the employer, or the user? And the use of copyrighted material and personal data to train AI systems has prompted legal challenges and debates about fairness.
Policy responses
Governments, businesses, and educational institutions are considering a range of responses.

Education and training are the most frequently discussed. Only by investing in education and training can societies ensure that the benefits are widely shared. This includes not only teaching technical skills but also strengthening abilities that complement AI, such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and adaptability. Because technology is changing rapidly, many experts emphasize lifelong learning: the idea that education should not end in early adulthood but continue throughout people's careers.

Social safety nets are another focus. Unemployment insurance, support for workers moving between jobs, and portable benefits that are not tied to a single employer could reduce the hardship of transitions. Some have proposed more radical measures, such as a universal basic income, a regular payment to all citizens regardless of employment. Such proposals remain controversial, with debates centering on cost, effects on work incentives, and political feasibility.

Regulation is a third area. Governments are developing rules on transparency, safety, data protection, and the use of AI in high-stakes decisions such as hiring, lending, and medical care. Finding the right balance between protecting people and allowing beneficial innovation is a difficult challenge.
What individuals can do

For individual workers, uncertainty about the future can be a source of considerable anxiety. While no one can predict the future precisely, several strategies seem sensible. Learn to use AI tools in your own field, since workers who can use these tools effectively are likely to be more valuable than those who cannot. Focus on developing skills that are difficult to automate, such as complex problem-solving, judgment in uncertain situations, and the ability to build trust with other people. Cultivate deep knowledge of a particular domain, since AI tools are most useful in the hands of people who understand the subject well enough to evaluate the output critically. And remain adaptable, since the ability to learn new things may itself be the most important skill of all.
Conclusion

The future of work in an age of artificial intelligence is genuinely uncertain. Optimists foresee an era of unprecedented productivity, in which machines take over tedious tasks and humans are free to pursue more meaningful work. Pessimists warn of widespread job losses, growing inequality, and social disruption. The most likely outcome probably lies somewhere between these extremes, and it will vary greatly across occupations, industries, and countries.

What seems clear is that the outcome is not predetermined. The choices made by companies, workers, educators, and governments over the coming years will significantly shape whether AI becomes a tool that empowers people or one that leaves many behind. History suggests that technological change, managed wisely, can raise living standards enormously. It also suggests that managing it wisely is never automatic.

items.title: Why Cities Look the Way They Do
items.zh: 城市为什么长成现在这个样子
items.summary: 从古代城市到汽车时代的郊区扩张，从分区规划、高速公路到住房危机和"十五分钟城市"，解释城市形态背后的经济、交通和政策原因。大学阶段城市与社会类学术词汇。
paras: Walk through the center of Paris, and you will find narrow streets lined with five- and six-story buildings, cafés on every corner, apartments above shops, and a metro station within a few minutes' walk of almost anywhere. Drive through the suburbs of Phoenix, Houston, or the Inland Empire in Southern California, and you will find wide roads, single-family houses on separate lots, shopping centers surrounded by enormous parking lots, and very few people walking anywhere at all.

These two kinds of urban environment are not the result of chance, nor simply of cultural preference. They are the product of geography, technology, economics, and, above all, deliberate policy decisions made over many decades. Understanding why cities look the way they do helps explain some of the most pressing issues facing urban residents today, from traffic congestion and long commutes to the soaring cost of housing.
Cities before cars

For almost all of human history, cities were shaped by the speed at which people could walk. Ancient Rome, medieval Venice, and nineteenth-century London were all dense, compact places, because most residents needed to reach their work, markets, and places of worship on foot. Rich and poor lived in close proximity, sometimes in the same building, with wealthier families occupying the lower floors and poorer ones the upper floors, which were harder to reach before elevators existed. Shops, workshops, and homes were mixed together.

The first major technology to reshape the city was the railway, and later the streetcar. In the late nineteenth century, electric streetcars allowed middle-class families to live several miles from their workplaces. "Streetcar suburbs" grew along the transit lines, with houses clustered within walking distance of each stop. Many of the most desirable neighborhoods in older American cities today, with their tree-lined streets and small local shopping districts, were originally built in this way.

It was not until the twentieth century that the car began to reshape the city. The automobile freed people from fixed transit routes, allowing development to spread in every direction. Built around the automobile, many American suburbs are almost impossible to navigate on foot.
The postwar transformation
The most dramatic transformation of the American city took place after the Second World War. Several forces combined to produce rapid suburban growth.

Federal housing policy made it easier than ever for families to buy homes, by insuring long-term mortgages with low down payments. These programs, however, overwhelmingly favored new single-family houses in suburban areas, and for decades they systematically excluded many Black families through a practice known as "redlining," in which neighborhoods with Black residents were marked as high-risk and denied access to mortgage lending. The consequences of these policies for racial segregation and wealth inequality persist to this day.

At the same time, the federal government funded the construction of the Interstate Highway System, a vast network of high-speed roads that made it possible to commute long distances by car. In many cities, highways were deliberately routed through existing neighborhoods, often those inhabited by poor and minority residents, demolishing thousands of homes and dividing communities.

Meanwhile, rising incomes, cheap gasoline, and mass-produced cars made automobile ownership accessible to most families. Developers built enormous housing tracts on inexpensive land at the edge of cities. Shopping moved from downtown streets to suburban malls. Offices and factories followed. The result was a new urban form: low-density, car-dependent, and spread over vast areas. Nowhere is this more visible than in the sprawling metropolitan areas of the American West.
The role of zoning

Perhaps the most important, and least visible, factor shaping modern cities is zoning. Zoning laws divide land into districts and specify what may be built in each one: what kinds of buildings, how tall, how large, and for what purposes.

Zoning originated in the early twentieth century, partly to protect residents from the noise and pollution of factories. Separating heavy industry from homes was a reasonable goal. Over time, however, zoning rules became far more extensive. In many American cities, a large majority of residential land is zoned exclusively for detached single-family houses, meaning that it is illegal to build apartments, townhouses, or even duplexes there. Zoning codes frequently require minimum lot sizes, minimum numbers of parking spaces, and maximum building heights, and they often prohibit shops and offices in residential areas.

These rules have profound effects. By requiring large lots and separating homes from shops and workplaces, they make it almost impossible to live without a car. By limiting the number of homes that can be built on a given area of land, they restrict the supply of housing. And by keeping apartments out of affluent neighborhoods, they can reinforce economic and racial segregation, a practice sometimes called "exclusionary zoning."
The housing affordability crisis

In many of the world's most economically successful cities, from San Francisco and New York to London, Sydney, and Vancouver, housing has become extraordinarily expensive. In some cities, the median home price is more than ten times the median household income. Many younger people find that they cannot afford to buy a home, or even to rent near their work, and must either spend a large share of their income on housing or endure long commutes from more affordable areas.

Economists broadly agree that a central cause of this crisis is a shortage of housing supply relative to demand. When a city's economy grows and attracts new workers, demand for housing rises. If the number of homes cannot increase sufficiently, because of zoning restrictions, lengthy approval processes, neighborhood opposition, or high construction costs, prices rise instead. This helps explain why housing in many cities has become so expensive.

Opposition to new development is often described by the term "NIMBY," which stands for "Not In My Back Yard." Existing residents may oppose new apartment buildings because of concerns about traffic, parking, neighborhood character, or property values. These concerns can be understandable, but the cumulative effect of such opposition can be to make cities unaffordable for teachers, nurses, service workers, and young families. In response, a movement sometimes called "YIMBY" ("Yes In My Back Yard") has emerged, advocating for zoning reform and more housing construction. Several cities and states have recently legalized duplexes and small apartment buildings in areas that were previously restricted to single-family homes.
Gentrification

A related and contested phenomenon is gentrification, the process by which wealthier residents move into a historically lower-income neighborhood, often leading to rising rents, new businesses, and changes in the neighborhood's character. Supporters point out that gentrification can bring investment, reduce crime, and improve services. Critics argue that it can displace long-term residents, especially renters, who can no longer afford to live in the communities they helped build. Research suggests that the effects vary considerably, and that the degree of displacement depends heavily on local housing supply and on policies such as tenant protections and affordable housing requirements.
The costs of car dependence

Car-dependent urban development has significant costs. Driving is the dominant form of transportation in most American metropolitan areas, and households spend a substantial share of their income on owning and operating vehicles. Traffic congestion wastes time and fuel. Transportation is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions. Road traffic accidents kill tens of thousands of people in the United States every year, and pedestrian deaths have risen significantly in recent years. Studies have also linked car-dependent environments to lower levels of physical activity.

A phenomenon known as "induced demand" complicates efforts to solve congestion by building more roads. When a highway is widened, travel initially becomes faster, which encourages more people to drive, to drive more often, or to move farther away. Within a few years, traffic frequently returns to its previous levels. Many transportation researchers therefore argue that adding road capacity is, by itself, an ineffective long-term solution to congestion.

European cities, by contrast, developed long before the automobile and often retained their dense historic cores. Many European countries also invested heavily in public transit and implemented policies that made driving more expensive, such as high fuel taxes and limited parking. As a result, residents of many European cities can meet most of their daily needs by walking, cycling, or public transportation. This is not to say that European cities have avoided suburban sprawl entirely; many have not. But the contrast illustrates how policy choices shape urban form.
Rethinking the city
In recent decades, urban planners have increasingly questioned the car-centered model. Several ideas have gained influence.
Mixed-use development encourages homes, shops, offices, and public spaces to be located close together, so that people can meet more of their needs nearby.
Transit-oriented development concentrates housing and businesses around train and bus stations, making public transportation more convenient and more financially viable.
Complete streets are designed to accommodate pedestrians, cyclists, public transit, and cars safely, rather than prioritizing vehicle speed above all else.

The "fifteen-minute city," a concept popularized by the urban scientist Carlos Moreno and adopted in various forms by cities such as Paris, envisions neighborhoods in which residents can reach most daily necessities, including groceries, schools, healthcare, parks, and workplaces, within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride.

These ideas are not without critics. Some argue that they are unrealistic in regions that have already been built around the car, that they may raise property values and accelerate gentrification, or that they impose particular lifestyles on residents who prefer space and privacy. Others note that many people genuinely value large homes, gardens, and quiet streets, and that suburban living remains popular. Any serious approach to urban planning must balance these competing preferences.
A tale of two commutes

The practical consequences of these choices are easy to see in the daily lives of ordinary workers. Consider two people with similar jobs. The first lives in a dense European city. She walks five minutes to a tram stop, rides for twenty minutes while reading, and walks a few more minutes to her office. On the way home, she buys groceries at a small shop near her apartment. She does not own a car, and her transportation costs are modest.

The second lives in a fast-growing suburb in the American Southwest, chosen because housing there is cheaper than in the city where he works. He drives forty-five miles each way on a congested freeway. On a good day, the trip takes an hour; when there is an accident, it can take two. He spends a significant share of his income on car payments, insurance, gasoline, and maintenance. There is no grocery store within walking distance of his home, and his children cannot safely walk or cycle to school.

Neither person made an irrational decision. Each responded sensibly to the options available. But those options were shaped long before they were born, by highway plans, zoning maps, and mortgage rules. This is perhaps the most important lesson of urban history: individual choices are always made within a built environment that someone else designed.
New pressures

Cities also face emerging challenges. Climate change brings risks of extreme heat, flooding, and wildfires, prompting investment in tree planting, cool roofs, flood defenses, and stricter building codes. The rise of remote work since the pandemic has reduced demand for downtown office space in many cities, raising questions about the future of central business districts and prompting proposals to convert empty offices into housing. And global migration continues to bring millions of new residents to cities every year, particularly in Asia and Africa, where the scale of urban growth is unprecedented.
Conclusion

Cities are among humanity's greatest inventions. They concentrate talent, ideas, and opportunity, and they generate a disproportionate share of economic growth and cultural innovation. But their physical form is not natural or inevitable. The wide roads, parking lots, single-family subdivisions, and expensive downtown apartments that we take for granted are the result of specific technologies and, above all, specific laws and policies. What was designed can be redesigned. The choices that today's residents, planners, and politicians make about zoning, transportation, and housing will shape how people live, work, and move for generations to come.
